passage:
Every evening on the school steps in Sultanpur, Nikita told anyone who would listen, "I'm going to fail physics. I'll get maybe twenty." Her friend Ramesh raised an eyebrow. "You haven't opened chapter six." "What's the point? If I expect the worst, I won't be sad." She shut the book and picked at her nails.
On result day she got sixty-four. "See?" she said, grinning with relief. "Lucky. I expected twenty."
Ramesh walked with her in silence. Then he said, "You skipped half the syllabus because you'd decided you'd fail. What would you have got if you hadn't?"
Nikita's smile faltered. "I don't know," she said. "I never found out."

qa.q: What mark did Nikita expect to get in physics?
qa.a: Nikita expected maybe twenty.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she said that if she expects the worst she won't be sad?
qa.a: Nikita was afraid of disappointment and protecting herself from it, so she lowered her expectations as a shield.

qa.q: What could Nikita try before the next exam?
qa.a: Nikita could open chapter six and work one topic a day, while still expecting some nerves. Studying first would let her find out what her real result could be.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Nikita's habit of predicting failure?
qa.a: Ramesh seems to see that it quietly cuts her effort, since she skipped half the syllabus. He asks what she might have got if she had tried.

grounding: A teenager expects the worst on every exam so any result feels like a win, though it quietly reduces effort.

passage:
The night before the history exam, Leila wrote FAIL, FAIL, MAYBE PASS on the back of her hand. "Realistically, I'll get a D," she told Hiroshi over the video call. "That way any grade is good news." She spent the evening on the first two topics, then scrolled her phone.
Hiroshi rubbed his eyes on the screen. "You haven't touched the last three."
"Because I'll fail anyway."
"You say that every time. And every time you got a B."
Leila looked at the words on her hand. She hadn't thought of it that way. Slowly she pulled the textbook closer. "One more hour," she said. "Just the third topic."
Hiroshi grinned. "I'll read mine at the same time."

qa.q: What did Leila write on the back of her hand?
qa.a: Leila wrote FAIL, FAIL, MAYBE PASS on the back of her hand.

qa.q: Why does Leila say she will get a D?
qa.a: Leila is anxious about being disappointed, so expecting the worst is a shield: any grade then feels like good news.

qa.q: What small step did Leila take after the video call?
qa.a: Leila agreed to study one more hour on the third topic, with Hiroshi reading his notes at the same time.

qa.q: What might Hiroshi have been thinking as he pointed out the B grades?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably thought that Leila's predictions were not matching her real results, and wanted to nudge her without lecturing.

grounding: A teenager expects the worst before exams so any result feels like a win, which can quietly reduce effort.

passage:
Monday: "I'm going to fail the chemistry test," Sabina announced at lunch. "Totally, definitely." Harsha rolled her eyes. "You say that every time." Sabina felt oddly calm saying it, like putting on armour.
Wednesday, the night before: Harsha was revising the last chapter at the library. Sabina skipped it. "What's the point? I'll fail anyway." She watched a cooking video instead and went to bed early.
Friday: Results. Sabina got 71. She laughed with relief. "See? Better than I thought!" Then Harsha showed her paper: 86. Most of the extra marks came from the last chapter. Sabina looked at her own blank answer on that page. The relief went a little sour. "I didn't even try that part," she said slowly.

qa.q: What did Sabina score on the chemistry test?
What was Sabina feeling when she saw Harsha's marks?
qa.a: Her relief turned a little sour; she felt regretful, noticing she had skipped the last chapter because she expected to fail.

qa.q: What small step could Sabina try before the next test?
qa.a: She could keep her low expectations if they calm her, but still revise every chapter, so the armour doesn't quietly cut her effort.

qa.q: How does Harsha see Sabina's 'I'm going to fail' habit?
qa.a: Harsha finds it familiar and a bit tiresome, rolling her eyes because Sabina says it every time.

grounding: Shows a teenager expecting the worst to protect her feelings, and seeing that it also quietly reduced her effort.

passage:
"Pankaj, you keep saying 'I'll fail, I'll fail,'" said Uday mama, settling into the cane chair. "Let me tell you about me at fifteen. Before every exam I'd tell my mother, 'I'll get zero.' Then I'd get fifty and feel like a king. It felt safe. If I expected nothing, nothing could hurt me.
But here's what I didn't tell anyone. I stopped studying the hard chapters. Why bother, if I was going to fail? In Class 10 I got a decent mark, but not enough for the science stream I wanted.
My maths teacher, Mr. D'Souza, called me in. He said, 'You protect yourself from disappointment, Uday, but you also protect yourself from trying.' That stung. The next year I stopped saying zero and started asking him for help on the hard chapters instead."

qa.q: What would Uday mama tell his mother before every exam?
qa.a: He'd say, 'I'll get zero.'

qa.q: Why did expecting zero feel safe to young Uday?
qa.a: It protected him from feeling hurt or disappointed, so any mark made him feel like a king.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Uday mama's story?
qa.a: Mr. D'Souza telling him he protected himself from trying as well as from disappointment; after that he stopped saying zero and asked for help.

qa.q: How might Mr. D'Souza have seen Uday's habit?
qa.a: He seemed to see a capable student quietly holding back effort, and cared enough to name it honestly.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how expecting the worst on exams shielded his feelings but quietly reduced his effort.

passage: The morning of the physics practical, the rain was so heavy the school bus broke down halfway, and Jyoti and Jeevan had to squeeze into a crowded shared auto. "I'm going to mess up the pendulum," Jyoti said, water dripping from her hair. "I'll forget the formula. I'll get the lowest marks." Jeevan grinned. "You say that before everything." "It works. Then anything is a bonus." In the lab, Jyoti's readings were neat. But when the examiner asked about the error calculation, she froze. She hadn't practised it. The night before, she'd thought, "I'll do badly anyway, why bother." She got a decent mark. Walking out, she felt relieved and then annoyed with herself. "I think my 'I'll fail' thing made me skip the one part that mattered," she said. Jeevan nodded. "Next time, say it and study anyway."

qa.q: What did Jyoti freeze on?
qa.a: The error calculation, when the examiner asked about it.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel walking out of the lab?
qa.a: She felt relieved at first, then annoyed with herself for skipping the part that mattered.

qa.q: What would you advise Jyoti before her next practical?
qa.a: She can keep her worst-case talk if it calms her, but still practise every part, including the hard ones.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see Jyoti's habit?
qa.a: Jeevan finds it familiar and a little funny, but sees clearly that it made her skip preparation.

grounding: Shows a teenager expecting the worst to protect her feelings, and noticing it also quietly reduced her effort.

passage: Before every exam Gargi announced her doom. "I'm going to fail chemistry. Like, properly fail." On the school bus through Lajpat Nagar she said it again, headphones round her neck. Damini rolled her eyes. "You said that about physics and got seventy-eight." "Exactly. Expect the worst, and then seventy-eight feels like a party." It worked, sort of. Gargi never cried over results. But Damini had noticed something: last night, when the group call went through organic reactions, Gargi logged off at nine. "No point, I'm failing anyway." Today the paper had three organic questions. Gargi came out pale. "That's fine," she said quickly. "I knew I'd fail." But her voice cracked on "knew", and she didn't wait to compare answers.

qa.q: What mark did Gargi get in physics?
qa.a: She got seventy-eight.

qa.q: What did Gargi's cracking voice after the paper suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was more upset and disappointed than she admitted, even though she had told herself to expect the worst.

qa.q: What could Gargi try before the next exam?
qa.a: She could keep her low expectations if they calm her, but still stay for the whole revision call, so low hopes don't turn into low effort.

qa.q: How might Damini see Gargi's doom talk now?
qa.a: Damini found it tiresome at first, but after last night she worries it is quietly costing Gargi real study time.

grounding: Shows a teenager expecting the worst before every exam to protect her feelings, and how that shield quietly cuts her effort.
